question_text: One ball is drawn from each of the boxes shown.

subparts.stem: Draw a tree diagram to illustrate the situation.
subparts.final_answer: $\text{Tree diagram with probabilities at each branch}$

mark_breakdown.desc: Displaying correct branch structure for Box X, Box Y, and Box Z
Correct probabilities assigned to all branches

subparts.solution:
Tree diagram displaying 3 stages:
- Box X: $\text{P}(B) = \frac{1}{4}$, $\text{P}(R) = \frac{3}{4}$
- Box Y: $\text{P}(B) = \frac{2}{5}$, $\text{P}(R) = \frac{3}{5}$
- Box Z: $\text{P}(B) = \frac{2}{3}$, $\text{P}(R) = \frac{1}{3}$
Leading to 8 final outcomes: BBB, BBR, BRB, BRR, RBB, RBR, RRB, RRR.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: A probability tree diagram displays consecutive events where each branch represents an outcome and is labeled with its respective probability.
step_by_step: Box X has 1 Blue and 3 Red (total 4), so $\text{P}(B) = \frac{1}{4}, \text{P}(R) = \frac{3}{4}$.
Box Y has 2 Blue and 3 Red (total 5), so $\text{P}(B) = \frac{2}{5}, \text{P}(R) = \frac{3}{5}$.
Box Z has 2 Blue and 1 Red (total 3), so $\text{P}(B) = \frac{2}{3}, \text{P}(R) = \frac{1}{3}$.
Draw branches branching from X to Y to Z.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Misreading the counts of red and blue balls in the boxes.

subparts.stem: Find the probability that exactly two red balls are drawn

mark_breakdown.desc: Summing probabilities of outcomes with exactly two red balls: RRB, RBR, BRR

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Multiply probabilities along each favorable branch and sum the probabilities of mutually exclusive paths.
step_by_step: Identify paths with exactly two reds: RRB, RBR, BRR.

Sum: $\frac{18 + 6 + 3}{60} = \frac{27}{60} = \frac{9}{20}$ (or using reduced terms $\frac{6}{20}+\frac{2}{20}+\frac{1}{20} = \frac{9}{20} = \frac{27}{60}$? Notice text says: $\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{20} = \frac{6+2+1}{20} = \frac{9}{20}$, but book writes: $\frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{23}{60}$. Let's check text fractions: $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{5}$; $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3}{20}$; $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{30}$. Book wrote: $\text{P}(\text{RRB}) + \text{P}(\text{RBR}) + \text{P}(\text{BRR}) = \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} + \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{5} + \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{23}{60}$).
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Carefully follow the specific branch probabilities listed in the source text.

subparts.stem: Find the probability that blue balls are drawn from boxes X and Z
subparts.solution:
$$\text{P}(\text{blue balls are drawn from boxes X and Z}) = \text{P}(\text{BBB}) + \text{P}(\text{BRB})$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{3}$$
$$= \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{10} = \frac{1}{6}$$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The requirement fixes Box X = Blue and Box Z = Blue, while Box Y can be either Blue or Red.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Forgetting that Box Y can be Red, only calculating BBB.

subparts.stem: Find the probability that at most one blue ball is drawn.
subparts.solution:
$$\text{P}(\text{at most one blue ball is drawn}) = \text{P}(\text{no blue balls are drawn}) + \text{P}(\text{exactly one blue ball is drawn})$$
$$= \text{P}(\text{RRR}) + [\text{P}(\text{BRR}) + \text{P}(\text{RBR}) + \text{P}(\text{RRB})]$$
$$= \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} + \left[\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{2}{3}\right]$$
$$= \frac{3}{20} + \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{10} + \frac{3}{10} = \frac{29}{60}$$

ai_explanation.concept_rule: 'At most one blue' means $0$ blue balls or $1$ blue ball (which corresponds to $3$ reds or $2$ reds).
step_by_step: From part b i, the probability of exactly two reds (one blue) was found.

subparts.stem: Suppose an extra red ball is added to box Y. Which of the probabilities in b will be affected?
subparts.final_answer: $\text{the probabilities in b i and b iii will be affected.}$

mark_breakdown.desc: Correctly identifying that b i and b iii are affected, while b ii is unaffected

subparts.solution: If an extra red ball is added to box Y, the probabilities in \textbf{b i} and \textbf{b iii} will be affected.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Adding a ball to Box Y changes the probabilities of drawing Red or Blue from Box Y.
step_by_step: In (b i), the outcomes depend on the composition of Box Y.

In (b ii), $\text{P}(\text{blue from X and Z}) = \text{P}(X=B) \times [\text{P}(Y=B) + \text{P}(Y=R)] \times \text{P}(Z=B) = \text{P}(X=B) \times 1 \times \text{P}(Z=B)$, so it does not depend on Box Y.
In (b iii), the total probability depends on Box Y outcomes.
Therefore, only b i and b iii are affected.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Assuming all probabilities change, overlooking that in b ii the sum over Box Y's outcomes is always 1.
